analysis.one_liner: Requires large data centers to disclose power and water use and pay their own infrastructure costs instead of ratepayers.
analysis.headline: The Ratepayer Bill of Rights Act was introduced on August 24, 2026 with 4 Democratic cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where no action has been taken since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets large data centers — those drawing at least 50 megawatts of electricity or 100,000 gallons of water a day. It would require them to publicly report their electricity and water use, the cost of the power lines and pipes built for them, and any public subsidies they receive. It would bar companies from shifting those project costs onto households, farms, and small businesses through utility rates, and would require independent studies showing a new data center won't strain local water or grid reliability. It also guarantees public notice, local meetings, and a complaint and refund process.
analysis.who_benefits: Households, farmers, ranchers, small businesses, schools, and hospitals that pay electric and water bills and would otherwise absorb part of the cost of infrastructure and resource demands driven by large data centers. Communities near proposed data centers gain advance notice, public meetings, and plain-language information before projects are approved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Utility customers and communities near data centers

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that protected ratepayers — households, farmers, ranchers, small businesses, schools, hospitals — have the right not to subsidize a covered data center: the company must pay all project-driven costs, sign a binding cost-recovery agreement, post financial security before construction, and refund any improper charge with interest within 90 days.

Ratepayers gain disclosure of projected and actual electricity and water use, infrastructure costs, effects on bills, and any public assistance the company received, posted to a searchable public database that confidentiality contracts cannot block.

Before final approval, independent assessments must confirm a data center will not materially reduce grid reliability or leave insufficient water for households, agriculture, and existing businesses during droughts, and residents get at least 60 days' notice and a local public meeting.

analysis.who_pays: Large data center operators — typically hyperscale tech companies — would bear the full cost of the transmission lines, water systems, and conservation measures built for their facilities, plus compliance and reporting costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large data center operators and tech companies

drawbacks.text: The bill layers new federal reporting, assessment, and cost-recovery requirements on data center projects administered across four agencies (FERC, DOE, EPA, and Labor) within their existing jurisdictions, which could slow projects and add compliance costs; communities competing for data center investment may see companies build elsewhere.

The bill does not change who sets utility rates: state and local authorities retain jurisdiction over rates, water rights, land use, and permitting, so the federal cost-shifting ban depends on how the federal rules interact with existing state systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary ratepayers the upside is direct: data centers are driving rapid growth in electricity and water demand, and the bill's stated aim is that families and small businesses stop absorbing those costs through their bills. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry — data center operators pay their own way — with some risk that disclosure and assessment requirements slow projects or push them to other locations. The design is narrow (50 MW / 100,000 gallons per day threshold) and leaves state ratemaking intact, which limits disruption but also limits federal reach over the actual setting of rates.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Cuellar introduced the Ratepayer Bill of Rights Act of 2026 in the House on August 24, 2026.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on Education and Workforce; the action history shows no further action, markup, or vote.
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large data center operators, which continue to build and contract for power and water without federal disclosure or cost-recovery requirements, and utilities that can still allocate project costs through existing state ratemaking.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data center operators and their utilities

for.name: Rep. Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full text of ten ratepayer rights on August 24, 2026.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 24, 2026 and has taken no action — no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for provisions in its jurisdiction and has taken no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats and no Republican cosponsors appear in the record; the bill has not reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits is recorded.

industries.industry: Large data centers / hyperscale tech companies
industries.note: The bill requires them to pay all project-driven infrastructure and water costs instead of spreading them across utility ratepayers, and to disclose use, subsidies, and emissions publicly. Those costs currently can be socialized through rates, so the shift moves billions in potential infrastructure expense from ordinary customers to the companies.

Utilities would gain customers from data center growth but lose the ability to recover project-driven transmission and generation costs from general ratepayers, and would face new disclosure of agreements and rate effects. State ratemaking authority is preserved, limiting the change.

Data centers drawing at least 100,000 gallons a day face independent water-availability assessments, no priority during emergencies, and conservation funding, which protects other water users but adds constraints on water sales and service commitments.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with four cosponsors, referred to two committees with no action for the remainder of a session ending January 3, 2027, is unlikely to reach a floor vote; most bills at this stage die in committee.
